title: We Never Really Have Time
coreMove: Treat plans as intentions, not property; you can influence future time without asking the future to reassure you before it arrives, and that is enough for sane action.

exampleSpecs.stakes: Douglas Hofstadter and Hofstadter's law expose why careful time estimates still meet hidden complexity.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show a careful estimate becoming an expectation rather than a possession.

exampleSpecs.stakes: The Sydney Opera House, Jorn Utzon, the 1959 construction start, and the 1973 opening show large plans escaping early confidence.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use a famous project overrun to separate blame from uncertainty.

exampleSpecs.audience: professionals counting on protected work blocks
exampleSpecs.stakes: David Cain's point about three hours and a subway breakdown makes future time feel less like an owned asset.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Make an expected work block collapse through ordinary interruption.

exampleSpecs.audience: savers trying to calm uncertainty with one more model
exampleSpecs.stakes: Blaise Pascal and the Pensees warn against turning a future plan into a demand for certainty.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show responsible saving becoming an impossible search for reassurance.

exampleSpecs.audience: parents trying to make a trip feel certain
exampleSpecs.stakes: David Cain's expected three hours and the subway breakdown logic transfer to travel plans and future time.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Contrast careful preparation with the fantasy that preparation owns the outcome.

exampleSpecs.audience: public project managers reviewing schedule misses
exampleSpecs.stakes: The Sydney Opera House overrun gives a public mirror for complex work between a 1959 construction start and 1973 opening.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Turn a late project review away from simple blame and toward named variables.
